node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Everyday chance words
node.description: Use everyday words such as might, will, never, maybe, likely and unlikely to discuss chance.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Possible and impossible events
node.description: Classify simple events as possible or impossible in familiar contexts.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Certain and impossible events
node.description: Distinguish events that must happen from events that cannot happen.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Likely and unlikely language
node.description: Use likely and unlikely to compare the chance of familiar events.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare chance words
node.description: Order and compare chance words from impossible through unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Event descriptions
node.description: Describe an event clearly enough that its occurrence can be judged.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Outcome versus event
node.description: Distinguish a single outcome from an event that may include one or more outcomes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Fair and unfair chance situations
node.description: Judge simple chance situations as fair or unfair based on possible outcomes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Identify a trial
node.description: Recognise one repetition of a chance experiment as a trial.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Predict before a trial
node.description: Make a prediction about a chance experiment before observing the outcome.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Record trial outcomes
node.description: Record outcomes from repeated trials of a simple chance experiment.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Tally chance outcomes
node.description: Use tally marks or simple tables to count outcomes from chance experiments.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Compare predicted and observed outcomes
node.description: Compare predictions with observed outcomes after conducting chance trials.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Repeat trials for stability
node.description: Recognise that more repeated trials can make observed patterns more stable.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: List all outcomes
node.description: List all possible outcomes for simple chance situations without omission or duplication.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Organised sample spaces
node.description: Use organised lists, tables or diagrams to represent possible outcomes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Equally likely outcomes
node.description: Recognise when outcomes in a simple sample space are equally likely.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Favourable outcomes
node.description: Identify the outcomes in a sample space that satisfy a given event.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Event complement introduction
node.description: Recognise the complement of an event as outcomes where the event does not occur.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Mutually exclusive simple events
node.description: Recognise simple events that cannot happen at the same time in one trial.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample space checks
node.description: Check whether a sample space is complete, non-overlapping and appropriate for the situation.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Chance language orders likelihood
node.description: Chance words can be ordered from impossible to certain to compare likelihood qualitatively.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Events must be clear
node.description: An event should be described clearly enough that it is possible to decide whether it occurred.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: A trial has one observed outcome
node.description: Each trial of a simple chance experiment produces one observed outcome.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Repeated trials show variation
node.description: Outcomes can vary from trial to trial even when the same experiment is repeated.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: More trials stabilise patterns
node.description: With more trials, observed outcome proportions often become more stable.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample space lists possible outcomes
node.description: A sample space lists the possible outcomes for a chance situation.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Favourable outcomes define an event
node.description: An event can be described by the outcomes in the sample space that satisfy it.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Equally likely is not automatic
node.description: Outcomes are equally likely only when the chance mechanism gives each outcome the same chance.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Complement is not the event
node.description: The complement of an event is the set of outcomes where that event does not occur.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample spaces need no duplicates
node.description: A well-formed simple sample space should avoid missing outcomes and duplicate outcomes.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Likely means certain
node.description: Learner treats a likely event as if it must happen.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Impossible confused with unlikely
node.description: Learner describes very unlikely events as impossible even when they can occur.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: One trial proves likelihood
node.description: Learner treats the result of one trial as proof of what is likely in the long run.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: Sample space missing outcomes
node.description: Learner omits possible outcomes or includes duplicates when listing a sample space.

node.subject: Mathematics
node.label: All listed outcomes equally likely
node.description: Learner assumes all listed outcomes are equally likely even when the chance mechanism is uneven.

edge.rationale: Everyday chance words are foundational to qualitative chance language.
Possible and impossible are core chance-language categories.
Certain and impossible anchor the ends of the chance-language continuum.
Likely and unlikely support comparative chance descriptions.
Ordering chance words practices qualitative likelihood comparison.
Chance language depends on clear event descriptions.
Outcome-versus-event language supports more precise probability reasoning.
Fairness judgments use qualitative chance comparison in simple situations.
Identifying a trial is central to conducting chance experiments.
Predictions are a common component of simple chance investigations.
Recording outcomes is central to chance experiments.
Tallying outcomes supports organising repeated trial results.
Comparing predictions and observations is a common chance-experiment task.
Repeated trials show variation and emerging stability in chance experiments.
Listing all outcomes is central to sample-space reasoning.
Organised representations support complete sample spaces.
Equally likely outcomes connect sample spaces to probability models.
Favourable outcomes define events within sample spaces.
Complements partition a sample space into event and not-event outcomes.
Mutually exclusive events rely on understanding which outcomes can occur together in one trial.
Checking completeness and non-duplication improves sample-space reasoning.
Possible and impossible classifications build from everyday chance language.
edge.failure_signal: Learner uses chance words without deciding whether an event can occur.

edge.rationale: Certain and impossible reasoning extends possible/impossible event classification.
edge.failure_signal: Learner confuses must happen, might happen and cannot happen.

edge.rationale: Likely and unlikely apply to events that can occur but vary in likelihood.
edge.failure_signal: Learner calls an impossible event unlikely rather than impossible.

edge.rationale: Ordering chance words requires distinguishing likely, unlikely, certain and impossible language.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot order qualitative likelihood terms consistently.

edge.rationale: Clear event descriptions make qualitative likelihood judgments meaningful.
edge.failure_signal: Learner describes events so vaguely that occurrence cannot be judged.

edge.rationale: Outcome-versus-event distinction requires clear event descriptions.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats one outcome and a set of outcomes as the same idea.

edge.rationale: Fairness judgments often depend on whether outcomes or players have equal chances, though early fairness can be informal.
edge.failure_signal: Learner judges fairness by preference rather than chance structure.

edge.rationale: Identifying a trial requires understanding what chance situation and event are being observed.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot distinguish one trial from a whole experiment.

edge.rationale: Predictions use qualitative likelihood reasoning before observing outcomes.
edge.failure_signal: Learner predicts without linking to possible outcomes or likelihood.

edge.rationale: Recording outcomes requires recognising each trial and its result.
edge.failure_signal: Learner mixes multiple trials or records non-outcomes.

edge.rationale: Tallying chance outcomes organises recorded trial results.
edge.failure_signal: Learner records outcomes but cannot count frequencies consistently.

edge.rationale: Comparing predicted and observed outcomes requires recorded outcome frequencies.
edge.failure_signal: Learner compares prediction to memory rather than recorded results.

edge.rationale: Repeated trials extend comparison of predicted and observed outcomes across more data.
edge.failure_signal: Learner overgeneralises from very few trials.

edge.rationale: Listing all outcomes requires distinguishing possible single outcomes from events.
edge.failure_signal: Learner lists events rather than distinct possible outcomes.

edge.rationale: Organised sample spaces build from listing possible outcomes systematically.
edge.failure_signal: Learner cannot organise outcomes without omissions or duplicates.

edge.rationale: Judging equally likely outcomes requires a clear sample space and chance mechanism.
edge.failure_signal: Learner assumes outcomes are equally likely just because they are listed.

edge.rationale: Identifying favourable outcomes requires a represented sample space.
edge.failure_signal: Learner counts favourable outcomes without identifying the full outcome set.

edge.rationale: Complements are defined relative to the event outcomes and the full sample space.
edge.failure_signal: Learner treats the complement as an opposite word rather than non-event outcomes.

edge.rationale: Mutually exclusive events require understanding whether events can share outcomes in one trial.
edge.failure_signal: Learner thinks all different events are mutually exclusive.

edge.rationale: Checking a sample space requires an organised representation to inspect for omissions and duplicates.
edge.failure_signal: Learner accepts incomplete or duplicated sample spaces as valid.
